audience.notes: Australian couples in their 30s, AUD 150K+, often marrying abroad with a smaller guest list. The bride (or a bridesmaid or mother helping) is drawing up or approving the list. payload.search_intent: Informational: who to invite to a bridal shower (kitchen tea), how many, who decides, and how to handle the awkward cases without hurting anyone.
payload.angle: The calm, current guide to the bridal shower guest list, written as convention and advice, never as rules. Answer who, how many and who decides in the first 100 words, then handle the awkward middle (in-laws, work friends, partners and men) and the case nobody in the SERP covers: a destination wedding with a small guest list abroad, people who cannot travel, a shower at home vs near the wedding, and virtual guests. Close with a printable checklist that maps to a Wonderland Studio guest list. Use Australian language (kitchen tea, hens, maid of honour) with 'bridal shower' as the main term.
payload.answer_block: Draft for the writer (first 60 to 80 words, under the H1): Most bridal showers invite the women closest to the bride who are also invited to the wedding: the bridal party, mothers, sisters and grandmothers on both sides, and close friends. Twenty to forty guests is a common size. The host draws up the list, but the bride has the final say. A destination wedding changes the maths, so see the section on guests who cannot travel.
serp_gaps_to_win: No editorial top-3 page in any market answers the destination wedding case (small guest list abroad, guests who cannot travel, shower at home vs at the destination, virtual guests).
No current, structured guide in the AU top 3; results are forums, Facebook, Pinterest and a 2012 column.
No editorial printable checklist; the image pack shows demand for printable guest list sheets.
US-led answers ignore Australian terms (kitchen tea, hens) and Australian spelling.
Most sources frame etiquette as rules; nobody explains the reasoning so couples can choose.

outline.h2: Who to invite to a bridal shower
outline.answers: Who usually goes on the list, in order of priority, and why the shower list sits inside the wedding list.
must_include: Answer block within the first 100 words of the article (see answer_block).
A short tiered list: bridal party; mothers, sisters, grandmothers on both sides; the partner's close female relatives; close friends; close family friends.

The convention that everyone at the shower is also invited to the wedding, explained by the reason (a shower invitation implies a wedding invitation and comes with a gift). Framed as 'the convention most families follow', never 'the rule'.
The common exception: a work or office shower among colleagues who are not wedding guests, held separately.
Link the wedding guest list etiquette page and the guest list how-to with non-exact anchors.

outline.h2: Who hosts the bridal shower and who decides the guest list
outline.answers: Who draws up the list, who approves it, and how to handle a mother or future mother-in-law who wants to add names.
must_include: Host drafts, bride approves: the usual split.
Both mothers are normally asked for names on their side; give each a number rather than an open invitation.
Short script for saying no to an extra name kindly (one or two sentences).
Link /celebration-ideas/who-hosts-bridal-shower for hosting and costs; do not repeat its cost content.

outline.h2: How many guests to invite to a bridal shower
outline.answers: A sensible size and how venue, format and the wedding guest list set it.
must_include: Present 20 to 40 as a common range, not a target; smaller is normal for a small or destination wedding.
Size follows the venue and format (home afternoon tea vs hotel high tea vs restaurant private room).
Rough ratio idea: a shower usually draws a fraction of the wedding list; say so qualitatively unless the researcher finds a sourced figure.
Link /celebration-ideas/bridal-shower-planning for the timeline and venue choice.

outline.answers: The awkward middle: cousins, aunts, the partner's family, friends of the mothers, and colleagues.
must_include: One consistent line for both families (apply the same test to both sides so nobody feels slighted). This addresses the paying parent's fear of embarrassment.
Cousins and aunts: invite by closeness, not by category, but keep the same cut-off on both sides.
Work colleagues: invite those coming to the wedding; otherwise a separate office celebration.
Multiple showers: keep guest lists separate so nobody is asked for two gifts.
Plus-ones are not expected at a traditional shower; link plus-one etiquette for the wedding itself.

outline.answers: Whether partners and male friends belong on the list, briefly, then hand over to the sibling article.
must_include: Keep this section to about 150 words. Traditional showers were women only; co-ed showers are now common and the couple decides.

Link /should-men-be-invited-to-the-bridal-shower with a non-exact anchor such as 'whether to make it a co-ed shower' or 'our take on men at the shower'. Never use 'should men be invited to the bridal shower' or 'are men invited to bridal showers' as anchor text.
Note the difference from hens or a bachelorette, which has its own guest list logic; link the bachelorette etiquette page.

outline.h2: Bridal shower guest list for a destination wedding
outline.answers: Who to invite when the wedding is abroad with a smaller list, and what to do for people who cannot travel.
must_include: This is the invisible-work section. Show what changes: the wedding list may be 40 to 100 people abroad while the people who love the bride at home are more numerous.

Convention under pressure: the convention still applies, but explain the options honestly (shower for wedding guests only; a separate, gift-free celebration such as an afternoon tea or engagement drinks for people not invited abroad).
People who are invited but cannot travel (older relatives, young families, cost): the shower at home is often their main event; place it so they can attend.

Shower at home vs near the wedding: at home a few months before for the stay-at-home circle; at the destination as an optional brunch early in the wedding week, near where guests stay, not on the welcome party day.
Virtual guests: a video link for a grandmother or friend overseas; mail-ahead gifts; keep the gift-opening short on camera.
Older guests: accessible venue at home (lift, step-free, seating), timing that suits them. Ties to paying_parent fear of elderly guests left out.

Link /celebration-ideas/destination-bridal-shower for hosting steps (do not repeat its steps), /destination-weddings/destination-wedding-guest-attendance for who travels, /destination-weddings/destination-wedding-guest-guide, and /wonderland-concierge for the wedding week abroad (room blocks, transfers, events).
Soft CTA line here (Discovery Call) is the natural place.

outline.h2: Printable bridal shower guest list checklist
outline.answers: A usable list to copy or print.
must_include: A checklist of 10 to 14 lines as a markdown list or table: confirm wedding guest list first; agree size and venue; host drafts, bride approves; both mothers give names to a set number; same rule both sides; check the partner's side; decide co-ed or not; flag people who cannot travel to the wedding; plan a video link if needed; collect addresses, dietary needs and accessibility notes; send invitations four to six weeks ahead (as convention; researcher to confirm or soften); track RSVPs in one place.
Offer the same columns as a template: link /wedding-guest-list-template (cluster head) and /wonderland-studio for keeping the shower list next to the wedding list.
Writer flags a designed printable PDF as [[NEEDS: printable checklist PDF or Canva download from design team]].

outline.answers: Five short answers for PAA and FAQ schema.
must_include: Q1 Do you have to invite everyone from the bridal shower to the wedding? (convention yes, with the office shower exception)
Q2 Can you invite someone to the bridal shower who is not invited to the wedding? (generally avoided; offer a gift-free alternative)
Q3 How many people should be on a bridal shower guest list? (20 to 40 common; follows venue and wedding size)
Q4 Who makes the bridal shower guest list? (host drafts, bride approves, mothers contribute)
Q5 Should you have a bridal shower if most guests cannot travel to the wedding? (often yes, at home, for the people who will miss the wedding)
Answers of 40 to 70 words each, no colons in questions.
Etiquette framed as convention or advice throughout ('most families', 'usually', 'a common approach'), never 'rules' or 'must'. Avoid the word 'rules' in headings.

Persona fear coverage (topic-adapted): couple fear 2, planning from the other side of the world, is covered by the destination wedding section (guests who cannot travel, shower at home vs abroad, virtual guests). Paying parent fears are adapted as: nobody in the family embarrassed or left out (one consistent line for both sides, how to say no kindly) and older guests not stranded (accessible venue at home, video link). Couple fear 1 (wrong planner) is out of scope; touch it only through the Concierge link in the destination section.
Australian terms: kitchen tea (once, early, as the Australian name), hens, maid of honour. Australian spelling.
Answer block in the first 100 words.
A printable checklist section.
One sentence noting that the bridal shower and the hens are separate events with separate lists.

Consistency with the sibling: /should-men-be-invited-to-the-bridal-shower calls the shower-guests-are-wedding-guests point 'the one firm rule'. Our piece frames it as the near-universal convention. Do not contradict the sibling's substance; only the framing differs (see open_questions).
must_avoid: Exact-match anchors for keywords other pages own: 'should men be invited to the bridal shower', 'are men invited to bridal showers', 'who hosts a bridal shower', 'bridal shower planning', 'destination bridal shower', 'wedding guest list etiquette', 'wedding guest list template', 'how to make a wedding guest list'.

Repeating content from siblings: hosting costs (who-hosts page), the planning timeline (bridal-shower-planning page), destination shower hosting steps (destination-bridal-shower page), men pros and cons (sibling).

Competitor sources or links: The Knot, Zola, Emily Post, WeddingWire, Paperlust, Brides Diary, Reddit, Pinterest, Etsy. No external sources are needed for convention; the researcher may cite only an official or neutral source if a statistic is used.
Presenting 20 to 40 guests, or any number, as a fact from a source unless the researcher sources it; state it as a common range.
Wedded World plug or link (user instruction).

Links to /10-of-the-best-bridal-shower-games (duplicate of the games page), /bridal-shower-themes (old kitchen tea themes page), /the-guest-list-issue and /7-practical-tips-to-keep-your-wedding-guest-list-under-control (older overlapping guest list pages).
Em dashes, colons in headings, US spelling.
Bargain tips (DIY, cheapest venues) aimed at the anti-persona.
Gendered assumptions beyond the convention: write so it works for a bride and groom, two brides, or a couple sharing a shower.
